4: Run by hand, those commands leave a lot to you.

A bare two reads as fine on a ring that should block, so the kit prints expected and actual as number and name.
A file server looks like any other, so the inventory's role column decides where the datagram check runs.

5: For each in-scope device, the kit runs these checks.
The antivirus in normal, active mode.
Network protection and controlled folder access at the ring's stage from the plan, block or audit.
On servers, network protection allowed on the server; and on high-UDP roles, datagram processing off.
And each firewall profile on, with inbound blocked.
It runs the guide's event query too, and writes the device checks, the drift, the events and a summary.
Moving a ring from audit to block is a change to the plan file, under the same change record that changes the Intune policy.
The kit never changes a policy.

10: Here's what the prevention check proves, against nist's catalog.
Antivirus and real-time protection on, in active mode, supports malicious code protection.
The host firewall on with inbound blocked supports boundary protection.
Network protection and controlled folder access at the ring's stage supports configuration settings.
And tamper protection on, with tampering attempts counted, supports software and information integrity.
The indicators are fed-ramp's, as the guide maps them.
The records support these controls; the assessor decides them.
11: A ring moved to block in Intune but not in the plan: every device reports drift, so change the plan with the same change record.
Defender Antivirus in passive mode: network protection doesn't run; the antivirus mode check catches it.
Datagram processing on a domain controller, the performance risk Learn documents for high-UDP roles.
Tamper protection turned off locally, so settings drift silently.
And a device with no state file, which looks compliant by absence; the kit lists it.
